title: Time reversal of complex evolution on a quantum computer
abstract: The Boltzmann-Loschmidt dispute in 1876-1877 discussed the problem of time reversal of ther- malization from time reversible classical equations of motion. Here, 150 years later, we highlight this problem in the frame of quantum computing. A quantum protocol is proposed that allows to perform a time reversal of complex evolution in the regime of many-body quantum chaos with many qubits. The system represents an evolution of qubits on a square lattice with inter-qubit next-nearest static couplings with a driven pulsed magnetic field. The system entropy grows rapidly to maximal values but returns to initial small values after time reversal. This time reversal is shown to be stable with respect to quantum gate imperfections. However, similar to the Lorenz butterfly effect, there is the butterfly effect of qubit when inversion of only one qubit breaks time reversibility of the whole system. It is argued that this protocol is accessible to nowadays quantum computers and annealers with hundreds of qubits.
summary: This work proposes a quantum protocol to reverse complex, chaotic time evolution in a many-body qubit system, drawing a parallel to the historical Boltzmann-Loschmidt dispute. The protocol successfully restores the initial quantum state and entropy, demonstrating robustness against imperfections. Crucially, it highlights a 'butterfly effect' where local perturbations can destroy the global time-reversal symmetry.
main_problem: The paper addresses the problem of time reversal of thermalization, originally posed by the Boltzmann-Loschmidt dispute, within the modern context of quantum many-body systems.
main_result: A quantum protocol was proposed that successfully reverses complex, chaotic evolution, showing the system's entropy returning to its initial low value, and this reversal is robust against minor quantum gate imperfections.
method: The time reversal is achieved by applying a time-reversed evolution operator ($U_r$) over a period equal to the initial evolution time, and its success is quantified using fidelity and entropy measurements.
model_or_system: The model is the Time Reversal Kicked Ising (TIRKI) model, simulating qubits on a square lattice with next-nearest static couplings and driven by a pulsed magnetic field.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F(t)$), von Neumann entropy ($S_q$), and level spacing statistics of quasienergies ($\lambda$).
important_parameters: Quantum chaotic regime (characterized by RMT level spacing), the time return period ($2t_r$), and the strength of static imperfections ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the system can be simulated by current quantum computers or annealers with hundreds of qubits, and the analysis relies on the system being in a chaotic regime.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares level spacing statistics to Poisson and GOE distributions, confirming quantum chaos. Later figures illustrate the fidelity decay and the 'butterfly effect' when a single qubit inversion breaks time reversibility.
paper_structure: The paper first frames the classical Boltzmann-Loschmidt problem in quantum terms. It then details the TIRKI model and the time-reversal protocol using specific Hamiltonians and propagators. Key results are demonstrated by analyzing entropy growth, fidelity recovery, and the sensitivity to local perturbations (the butterfly effect).
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, physical realization of time reversal in a highly non-equilibrium, chaotic quantum many-body system, linking fundamental statistical mechanics debates to modern quantum computation feasibility.
